02 · Examination technique
Palpation, percussion, auscultation
Each method answers one question: is the tissue dense, airy or fluid-filled, and how does it conduct sound. The result is always compared with the symmetric point.
Four steps
Painful points:
both palms on symmetric areas; ribs, intercostal spaces, muscles, spinous processes. A rib fracture — crepitus; neuralgia — 3 painful points.
Resistance:
compression in the anteroposterior (sternum and interscapular area) and lateral directions. Increased in emphysema and exudative pleurisy.
Excursion:
palms on the lower lateral areas, thumbs beside the spine; on deep inspiration the fingers should move apart equally.
Vocal fremitus:

palms parallel to the ribs, the patient says “thirty-three” or “ninety-nine” in a low voice; the hands are then swapped. Increased — consolidation, cavity; decreased — fluid, air, emphysema; absent — obstructive atelectasis.
Finger on finger
The middle phalanx of the left 3rd finger (pleximeter) is pressed firmly to the skin, the other fingers are lifted.
With the right 3rd finger, tap twice, short and perpendicular, using only wrist movement.
Comparative:
moderate force; supraclavicular → clavicles → 1st–2nd spaces → axilla 4th–5th → suprascapular → interscapular (pleximeter vertical) → infrascapular 7th–9th.
Topographic:

quiet force; from clear sound toward dull; the border is marked at the edge of the pleximeter on the clear-sound side. Apices, Kronig's isthmus, lower borders along 7 lines, mobility (6–8 cm on the midaxillary line).
Percussion detects foci at a depth of 5–7 cm and larger than 2–3 cm, and pleural fluid over 300–500 mL.
With the stethoscope diaphragm
A quiet, warm room; the patient sitting or standing, undressed to the waist. The diaphragm is pressed firmly to the skin, not over clothing.
Deeper, even breathing through the mouth; 1–2 full cycles at each point.
The sequence is the same as in comparative percussion, left and right in turn.
Main breath sound → duration of expiration → adventitious sounds (type, phase, location).
Differentiate: asking the patient to cough, pressing the stethoscope, “false breathing” with the mouth and nose closed.
Bronchophony:
whispered “one-two-three”; increased — consolidation and cavity; decreased — fluid, air, atelectasis.

Clear lung sound
A loud, long-lasting, low-frequency sound. Heard over healthy lung.
Dull (femoral) sound
Quiet, very short, relatively high-frequency. Over airless tissue or fluid. Normally over the liver, the absolute cardiac dullness and the thigh muscles.
Impaired (dullish) sound
Between clear lung sound and dull sound: quieter and shorter. Over tissue with partly reduced air content.
Tympanic sound
A loud, long, musical (harmonic) sound resembling a drum. Over an air-filled cavity with non-tense walls. Normally over Traube's space and the trachea.
Hyperresonant (box-like) sound
Louder, lower and longer than clear lung sound, as when striking an empty box. When lung air content is increased.
Dull-tympanic sound
A shortened, quieter sound with a tympanic tinge. When air and fluid are present in the alveoli at the same time, over compressed (relaxed) lung.
Metallic sound
A ringing tympanic sound rich in overtones. Over a large (6–8 cm), smooth-walled, superficial cavity or a closed pneumothorax.
Cracked-pot sound
A rattling tympanic sound. Over a superficial cavity connected to a bronchus by a narrow slit; the patient keeps the mouth open.
A soft, low-frequency (mostly 100–400 Hz) sound: heard throughout inspiration and in the first third of expiration.
Diminished vesicular breathing
The same recording: by the time the sound reaches the chest wall it is attenuated by air, fluid or hyperinflation, and its high frequencies fade (−10 dB, frequencies above 350 Hz attenuated).
Harsh (intensified) breathing
Both inspiration and expiration are loud and uneven, and expiration is heard in full. When the bronchial mucosa is inflamed.
Saccadic (interrupted) breathing
Inspiration is split into 2–3 short parts: because of edema of the small bronchi the alveoli do not expand simultaneously.
Harsh, resembling an “h” sound, rich in high frequencies. Expiration is louder and longer than inspiration, with a pause between the phases.
Faint bronchial breathing
Breathing with a bronchial timbre but quiet. Over compressed lung (compression atelectasis).
Mixed (bronchovesicular) breathing
Inspiration resembles vesicular breathing, expiration resembles bronchial breathing. When consolidated foci are mixed with healthy tissue.
Amphoric breathing
Low, deep bronchial breathing with a metallic tinge, as when blowing across the mouth of an empty bottle. Over a large smooth-walled cavity connected to a bronchus.
No breath sounds are heard
Almost silence in the stethoscope: sound is not transmitted (fluid, air, closed bronchus).
Whistling dry rales
Continuous (longer than 100 ms), musical, high-pitched sounds; often several tones (polyphonic). Mainly in expiration. Narrowing of the small bronchi.
Rumbling dry rales
Continuous, low (about 200 Hz and below), snoring-like sound. Vibration of thick sputum in the large bronchi; changes after coughing.
Fine moist rales (small-bubble)
Short (under 10 ms), high-pitched, discontinuous crackles, mainly in mid and late inspiration. Small bronchi, bronchioles and alveoli.
Coarse moist rales (large-bubble)
Longer (over 10 ms), low, discontinuous sounds resembling “boiling”; at the beginning of inspiration and also in expiration. Fluid in the large bronchi and cavities.
Uniform, very fine crackles heard suddenly only at the peak of inspiration: like rubbing hair together near the ear. Not changed by coughing.
Pleural friction rub
Interrupted creaking in both phases (new leather, steps on snow). Close to the ear, intensifies when the stethoscope is pressed, and is heard even in “false breathing”.
Stridor
A high-pitched, monophonic sound heard mainly on inspiration; loudest over the neck. Narrowing of the larynx or trachea.
Fluid
Over fluid: femoral dullness, no breath sounds or fremitus.
Garland's triangle
Garland's triangle: between the spine, the Damoiseau line and a line drawn from its highest point to the spine. Compressed lung: dull-tympanic sound, faint bronchial breathing.
Rauchfuss–Grocco triangle
Rauchfuss–Grocco triangle on the healthy side: mediastinal organs displaced by the pressure of fluid give dullness.
Compressed lung (Skoda's zone)
increased, egophony
Compressed lung above the fluid level: dull-tympanic sound (Skoda), faint bronchial breathing, egophony.
Acute bronchitis
Acute inflammation of the bronchial mucosa. Because the lung tissue is not affected, percussion and vocal fremitus are unchanged: all the signs are on auscultation.
Acute diffuse inflammation of the tracheal and bronchial mucosa, mainly viral. The leading symptom is cough, which can last up to 3 weeks; there is no infiltration of the lung tissue.

Viruses (influenza, parainfluenza, RSV, rhinovirus, adenovirus, coronaviruses) — up to 90%; bacteria less often (Mycoplasma pneumoniae, Chlamydophila pneumoniae, Bordetella pertussis). Risk factors: smoking, chilling, dust and gases.

Edema and hyperemia of the mucosa, damage to the ciliated epithelium, increased secretion. Irregularity inside the bronchus and thick secretion produce dry rales, thinned secretion produces moist rales.
First a dry, painful (“scratching behind the sternum”) cough, after 2–3 days mucous or mucopurulent sputum. Low-grade fever, weakness, runny nose, sore throat. With bronchospasm: shortness of breath.
General condition is satisfactory, the chest is unchanged, and both sides take part equally in breathing. The respiratory rate may rise slightly.
Blood: unchanged or mild leukocytosis, ESR slightly raised. Sputum: mucous, leukocytes.
Chest X-ray unchanged (done to exclude pneumonia if there is fever above 38 °C, tachycardia, tachypnea or focal physical signs). With bronchospasm: spirometry.
Bronchopneumonia, bronchospasm (obstructive bronchitis), progression to chronic bronchitis.
Difference from pneumonia: no dullness on percussion, no bronchial breathing and no localized consonating moist rales; the rales are bilateral, scattered and change after coughing.
Dry stage (days 1–3)
The chest is unchanged and takes part symmetrically in breathing.
Painless, resistance normal, vocal fremitus unchanged.
Comparative: clear lung sound at all symmetric points. Topographic: borders and mobility normal.
Harsh breathing, prolonged expiration; bilateral scattered dry rumbling (large bronchi) and whistling (small bronchi) rales. Their number and location change after coughing.
Unchanged.
Moist stage (after the sputum thins)
Vocal fremitus unchanged.
Clear lung sound.
Harsh breathing; large- and medium-bubble non-consonating moist rales. They decrease or disappear after the sputum is coughed up.
Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD)
Persistent airway obstruction: chronic bronchitis and emphysema together. The physical picture shows a hyperresonant sound, prolonged expiration and dry rales.

A disease with long-lasting respiratory symptoms and airflow limitation that is not fully reversible and is usually progressive (GOLD 2026). The diagnosis is confirmed by post-bronchodilator spirometry with FEV1/FVC < 0.70.
The main factor is tobacco smoking (smoking index above 10 “pack-years”); indoor air pollution (biomass fuel), occupational dust and gases, alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency, childhood infections.

Chronic inflammation and fibrosis of the small bronchi, mucus hypersecretion + destruction of the alveolar walls (emphysema). In expiration the small bronchi collapse and air is trapped (hyperinflation): the chest widens and the diaphragm descends.
Chronic cough with morning sputum, progressive shortness of breath (first on exertion, then at rest), increased and purulent sputum during exacerbations.

Barrel chest, bulging supraclavicular fossae, accessory muscles are used, exhalation through pursed lips, the “tripod” position (leaning on a table). Bronchitic phenotype: diffuse cyanosis and peripheral edema (“blue bloater”); emphysematous phenotype: thin, pink, marked dyspnea (“pink puffer”).

Blood: secondary erythrocytosis (in hypoxemia), leukocytosis during an exacerbation. Eosinophils ≥300/µL: a high chance of response to inhaled glucocorticoids. Blood gases: hypoxemia, hypercapnia in the late stage.

Spirometry: FEV1/FVC < 0.70 (key), severity by FEV1. X-ray: increased lucency of the lung fields, flattened diaphragm, “hanging” heart. CT: emphysema type. Pulse oximetry, ECG (right ventricular strain).
Respiratory failure, chronic cor pulmonale, secondary polycythemia, pneumothorax (rupture of bullae), pneumonia.
Difference from bronchial asthma: constancy of symptoms, incomplete reversibility of obstruction, late onset and a smoking history. The physical signs are similar, so spirometry decides.
Bronchitic phenotype
Barrel chest, diffuse cyanosis, accessory muscles are used.
Resistance increased, excursion reduced, vocal fremitus slightly weakened.
Comparative: hyperresonant tinge. Topographic: lower borders lowered, mobility reduced.
Harsh or diminished breathing, prolonged expiration; dry rumbling and whistling rales, especially on forced expiration.
Slightly weakened.
slightly weakened
Emphysematous phenotype
Thin patient, pink complexion, marked dyspnea, exhales through pursed lips, barrel chest.
Resistance sharply increased, excursion small, fremitus weakened on both sides.
Hyperresonant sound; apices high, Kronig's isthmus wide, lower borders lowered by one rib, mobility reduced to 2–3 cm.
Bilaterally markedly diminished vesicular breathing, prolonged expiration; few rales.
Diminished.
Bronchial asthma
Attacks of reversible bronchial obstruction. In an attack: hyperresonant sound, prolonged expiration and whistling rales; in a severe attack, a “silent lung”.

A disease with chronic airway inflammation, manifesting as episodic wheezing, shortness of breath, chest tightness and cough, with variable, reversible airflow limitation that varies in time and intensity (GINA 2025).

Allergens (house dust mites, pollen, animal dander, mold), viral infections, physical exertion, cold air, smoke, NSAIDs (aspirin-induced asthma), occupational factors; hereditary predisposition, atopy.

Spasm of the bronchial smooth muscle, mucosal edema, thick sticky mucus (mucus plugs). The small bronchi narrow: air is trapped in expiration (acute hyperinflation), and the turbulent flow produces musical rales.

Attacks of suffocation, especially at night and in the early morning; expiration is difficult (expiratory dyspnea), chest tightness, dry cough, and at the end of the attack a small amount of sticky “glassy” sputum.

Forced position: sitting, leaning on the hands against the knees or a table (orthopnea). Accessory muscles are used, the intercostal spaces retract, the chest is fixed in the inspiratory position. A wheeze audible from a distance (“distant rales”). In a severe attack the patient cannot speak; cyanosis, paradoxical pulse.
Eosinophilia in blood and sputum; Curschmann spirals and Charcot–Leyden crystals in sputum. Total IgE is raised (atopic asthma). In a severe attack hypoxemia; normocapnia is a danger sign.

Spirometry: obstruction, FEV1 rising by ≥12% and ≥200 mL on the bronchodilator test. Peak flow: diurnal variability >10%. FeNO raised. Allergy tests. X-ray: increased lung air content during an attack.
Status asthmaticus, pneumothorax, mediastinal emphysema, atelectasis (mucus plug), respiratory failure.

Difference from cardiac asthma: age, allergic history, expiratory dyspnea, no moist rales in the lower parts; difference from COPD: reversibility and the disappearance of physical signs between attacks.
Attack
Orthopnea, expiratory dyspnea, accessory muscles, wheeze audible from a distance.
Resistance increased, excursion reduced, vocal fremitus weakened on both sides.
Comparative: hyperresonant sound. Topographic: lower borders lowered, mobility sharply reduced.
Diminished vesicular breathing, sharply prolonged expiration; numerous whistling dry rales over both lungs, mainly in expiration.
Severe attack: “silent lung”
The patient cannot speak, cyanosis, exhausted, shallow breathing. A life-threatening condition!
Excursion is almost absent, fremitus sharply weakened.
Hyperresonant sound.
Breath sounds and rales are barely audible: the airflow is so small that rales are not produced. The disappearance of rales is a sign of worsening, not improvement.
Sharply weakened.
sharply weakened
The “silent lung” is a sign of an emergency resuscitation situation.
Interval between attacks
Vesicular breathing; isolated whistling rales may be present on forced expiration.
Pulmonary emphysema
Persistent increase in lung air content with destruction of the alveolar walls: hyperresonant sound, lowered borders, diminished breathing on both sides.
Persistent enlargement of the air spaces distal to the terminal bronchioles with destruction of their walls. It most often occurs as part of COPD.
Smoking (centriacinar emphysema), alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency (panacinar, lower lobes, young patients), old age, occupational dust.

A protease–antiprotease imbalance destroys the elastic fibers. The elastic recoil of the lung decreases, the small bronchi collapse in expiration and air is trapped. The chest is fixed in the inspiratory position, and the diaphragm descends and flattens.
Gradually increasing expiratory dyspnea, cough with scanty sputum, weight loss.

Barrel chest: the anteroposterior dimension approaches the transverse, the ribs are horizontal, the intercostal spaces are wide, the epigastric angle is obtuse, the supraclavicular fossae bulge. Exhalation through pursed lips, accessory muscles active.
In the late stage hypoxemia and erythrocytosis; alpha-1 antitrypsin level (in young patients).

X-ray: translucent lung fields, low flat diaphragm, horizontal ribs, narrow cardiac shadow. CT shows the type of emphysema and bullae. Spirometry: obstruction, total lung capacity and residual volume increased, DLCO reduced.
Spontaneous pneumothorax (rupture of bullae), respiratory failure, chronic cor pulmonale.
A bilateral hyperresonant sound and diminished breathing are typical of emphysema; in pneumothorax the signs are unilateral and tympanic.
Clinical picture
Barrel chest, horizontal ribs, bulging supraclavicular fossae.
Resistance sharply increased, excursion reduced, vocal fremitus equally weakened on both sides.

Comparative: hyperresonant sound. Topographic: apices up to 5 cm above the clavicle in front and above C7 behind; Kronig's isthmus widened to 8–9 cm; lower borders lowered by one rib; mobility of the lower edge reduced to 1–2 cm. Absolute cardiac dullness is reduced or not detected.
Vesicular breathing equally diminished on both sides, expiration prolonged. If bronchitis is added: dry rales.
Diminished on both sides.
In emphysema the lung covers the heart: absolute cardiac dullness decreases or disappears.
Bronchiectasis
Irreversible dilatation and suppuration of the bronchi, most often in the lower lobes: localized medium and coarse moist rales, “mouthful” sputum in the morning.
A disease in which the bronchi are irreversibly dilated (cylindrical, varicose, saccular) as a result of destruction of their walls, manifesting as chronic purulent inflammation.

Severe childhood pneumonias, whooping cough, measles; cystic fibrosis, primary ciliary dyskinesia, immunodeficiency, allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis, bronchial obstruction (foreign body, tumor), tuberculosis.

The “vicious circle” of infection–inflammation–destruction: secretion accumulates in the damaged bronchus, microbes multiply, and the wall is destroyed further. Liquid pus in the dilated bronchi produces moist rales; fibrosis of the surrounding tissue produces localized dullness.
Chronic cough, especially in the morning and in the drainage position, with a “mouthful” of abundant purulent sputum (3 layers on standing), hemoptysis, fever and weakness during exacerbations.
Clubbed fingers (“drumsticks”) and watch-glass nails, weight loss, pallor, sometimes cyanosis. When the patient lies on the healthy side more sputum is produced (drainage position).
In an exacerbation leukocytosis, raised ESR, anemia. Sputum: purulent, with microflora (Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Haemophilus influenzae).

High-resolution CT is the gold standard (bronchial diameter larger than the adjacent artery, “signet ring sign”, bronchi do not taper toward the periphery). Bronchoscopy, spirometry, sweat test for cystic fibrosis.
Pulmonary hemorrhage, abscess, empyema, amyloidosis, chronic cor pulmonale, respiratory failure.
Difference from chronic bronchitis: localized and persistent moist rales, abundant purulent sputum, clubbed fingers.
Exacerbation (lower lobes)
Clubbed fingers; the affected side lags slightly in breathing.
Vocal fremitus in the affected area is unchanged or slightly increased (peribronchial fibrosis).
Impaired sound over the lower areas; mobility of the lower edge reduced.
Harsh breathing over the affected area, localized medium and coarse moist rales (persistent, in one place), dry rales. The rales decrease after the sputum is coughed up.
May be slightly increased.
Dilated bronchi
slightly increased
Lobar pneumonia
Lung tissue
Pneumonia occupying a whole lobe and also involving the pleura. Three stages: crepitation (I) — bronchial breathing and dullness (II) — resolving crepitation (III).
Acute infectious inflammation occupying one or several lobes of the lung (larger than a segment), filling the alveoli with fibrinous exudate and always involving the pleura as well (pleuropneumonia).
Mainly Streptococcus pneumoniae (pneumococcus, especially serotypes 1–3); less often Klebsiella pneumoniae (upper lobes, “currant jelly” sputum), Legionella.

I — stage of congestion (hyperemia), days 1–3: capillaries are full, air and exudate are present in the alveoli together. II — stage of hepatization, days 3–7: first red (erythrocytes, fibrin), then gray (leukocytes) hepatization; the alveoli are airless, the bronchi are patent. III — stage of resolution: the exudate dissolves and air returns to the alveoli. The physical signs reflect this morphology exactly.

Sudden severe chills with fever of 39–40 °C, stabbing pain on the affected side that worsens on breathing and coughing (pleurisy), cough first dry, then with “rusty” sputum, shortness of breath, weakness.

Febrile face, flushed cheek on the affected side, herpes on the lips and nose, flaring of the nostrils on breathing, tachypnea, cyanosis; the affected side lags in breathing. Because of the pain the patient lies on that side.

Neutrophilic leukocytosis (15–30·10⁹/L), left shift, toxic granulation, ESR and CRP sharply raised, procalcitonin raised. Sputum: fibrin, erythrocytes, Gram-positive diplococci. Blood culture, pneumococcal urinary antigen.
X-ray: homogeneous opacity bounded by a lobe or segment, air bronchogram; pleural reaction. Pulse oximetry. Severity assessment: CURB-65.
Parapneumonic pleurisy and empyema, abscess, infectious-toxic shock, acute respiratory failure, myocarditis, pericarditis, meningitis, sepsis, carnification.

Difference from exudative pleurisy: in stage II vocal fremitus and bronchophony are increased and bronchial breathing is heard (in pleurisy diminished or absent). Difference from obstructive atelectasis: the bronchus remains patent.
Stage I — congestion (days 1–3)
The affected side lags in breathing.
Pain; vocal fremitus slightly increased.
Dull-tympanic sound over the affected lobe; mobility of the lower edge reduced.
Diminished vesicular breathing; crepitation at the peak of inspiration (crepitatio indux). A pleural friction rub may be added.
Slightly increased.
Hyperemia, exudate + air
Crepitatio indux: the exudate on the alveolar walls separates at the end of inspiration.
Stage II — hepatization (days 3–7)
The affected side lags sharply in breathing, tachypnea.
Vocal fremitus increased.
Dull (femoral) sound over the whole lobe; mobility of the lower border is absent.
Pathological bronchial breathing; no rales (no air in the alveoli). With parapneumonic pleurisy: pleural friction rub.
Increased (pectoriloquy).
Hepatization: airless tissue
Stage III — resolution
The condition improves, the fever falls by crisis or lysis.
Vocal fremitus slightly increased, gradually normalizing.
Dull-tympanic sound, then clear lung sound.
Mixed or diminished vesicular breathing, resolving crepitation (crepitatio redux), fine consonating moist rales.
Resolution: air is returning to the alveoli
Crepitatio redux and consonating fine moist rales (a recording is available on the separate button below).
Focal pneumonia (bronchopneumonia)
Small foci involving a bronchus and the alveoli belonging to it. Localized consonating fine moist rales are the main physical sign.
Pneumonia occupying one or several lobules or segments, in which the inflammation passes from the bronchus to the alveoli. The exudate is serous-purulent, and the pleura is little involved.
Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae, Staphylococcus aureus, Moraxella catarrhalis, atypical pathogens (Mycoplasma, Chlamydophila), viruses; aspiration.

Foci of inflammation alternate with healthy air-filled tissue. Small foci may not be detected on percussion; when the foci merge (confluent), dullness appears. Liquid secretion in the bronchi surrounded by consolidated tissue produces consonating moist rales.
Develops gradually, often after an ARVI: fever of 38–38.5 °C, cough with mucopurulent sputum, weakness; little pain.
General condition of moderate severity, tachypnea; the chest is usually unchanged.
Moderate leukocytosis, raised ESR and CRP. Sputum bacterioscopy and culture.
X-ray: focal opacities with indistinct borders up to 1–1.5 cm in the lower lobes. CT shows small foci better.
Pleurisy, abscess, respiratory failure.
Difference from bronchitis: localized, persistent, consonating moist rales and (when foci merge) localized dullness.
Clinical picture (foci in the right and left lower lobes)
The chest is unchanged, or the affected side lags slightly in breathing.
Vocal fremitus is slightly increased over large or merged foci.
Unchanged over small foci; impaired sound over merged foci.
Mixed (bronchovesicular) or harsh breathing over the focus, fine consonating moist rales; dry rales (bronchitis).
Slightly increased over the focus.
Foci of inflammation
Consonating (ringing) fine moist rales: consolidated tissue conducts sound well.
Lung abscess
A purulent cavity in the lung. Before rupture: signs of consolidation; after rupture into a bronchus: signs of a cavity — tympanic sound, amphoric breathing, coarse moist rales.
Circumscribed purulent-necrotic destruction of lung tissue with formation of one or more cavities; a pyogenic capsule forms around it.

Aspiration (alcoholism, epilepsy, anesthesia, dysphagia) — anaerobic flora, Staphylococcus aureus, Klebsiella pneumoniae; bronchial obstruction (tumor, foreign body); septic emboli. Aspiration abscesses are most often in segments S2, S6 and S10 of the right lung.

Stage I (before rupture): purulent infiltrate — airless dense tissue. Stage II (after rupture into a bronchus): pus drains through the bronchus, and air and a fluid level appear in the cavity. A superficial cavity larger than 4 cm that communicates with a bronchus gives cavity signs.

Stage I: high hectic fever, chills, heavy sweating, dry cough, chest pain. On rupture: suddenly a “mouthful” of abundant (up to 0.5–1 L per day) foul-smelling purulent sputum, sometimes blood-stained; after that the fever falls and the condition improves.
Severe intoxication, pallor, the affected side lags in breathing; in the chronic course, clubbed fingers. Foul breath odor.
High neutrophilic leukocytosis, left shift, sharply raised ESR, anemia. On standing the sputum separates into 2–3 layers, with elastic fibers and many leukocytes.
X-ray: in stage I a round opacity; in stage II a cavity with a horizontal fluid level. CT: the wall and location of the cavity. Bronchoscopy (to exclude a tumor, for drainage).
Pyopneumothorax and pleural empyema, pulmonary hemorrhage, sepsis, brain abscess, gangrene, chronic abscess.

Difference from cavitary tuberculosis: tuberculosis is in the upper lobes, mycobacteria are found in the sputum, and the fluid level is small. Difference from a disintegrating tumor: the cavity wall is thick and irregular; CT and bronchoscopy.
Stage I — before rupture into the bronchus
Pain over the infiltrate; vocal fremitus increased (may be weakened in a large, deep abscess).
Impaired or dull sound over the infiltrate.
Diminished vesicular or bronchial breathing; if the pleura is involved, a pleural friction rub.
Increased.
Purulent infiltrate
Stage II — after rupture into the bronchus
The condition improved after the “mouthful” of sputum.
Vocal fremitus increased over the cavity.
Tympanic sound over the cavity; metallic sound over a large smooth-walled cavity, cracked-pot sound when it communicates through a narrow slit.
Amphoric breathing, coarse consonating moist rales. When the cavity fills with pus the signs weaken, and when it empties they reappear.
Cavity (air + fluid level)
Cavity signs are detected only if it is superficial, larger than 4 cm and communicates with a bronchus.
Perifocal infiltration
Pulmonary tuberculosis (infiltrative and cavitary)
Most often the apex and posterior segments of the upper lobes: dullness over the apex, a narrowed Kronig's isthmus, fine consonating moist rales; cavity signs over a cavern.
A chronic infectious disease caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis, with granulomatous inflammation, caseous necrosis and disintegration (cavity formation).
M. tuberculosis (Koch's bacillus), spread by the airborne route. Risk factors: HIV, diabetes mellitus, immunosuppressive therapy, alcoholism, malnutrition, close contact, silicosis.

Infiltrate appears in the well-aerated segments S1, S2 and S6 of the upper lobes. When caseous masses are expelled through the bronchus, a cavity forms. Fibrosis shrinks the apex and lung tissue: the apex descends and Kronig's isthmus narrows.
Prolonged (more than 3 weeks) cough, evening low-grade fever, night sweats, weight loss, weakness, hemoptysis. Often there are few symptoms.

Thinness, pallor, the “tuberculous face” (flushed cheeks, bright eyes). On the affected side the supraclavicular and infraclavicular fossae are sunken, the shoulder girdle muscles are atrophic, and the chest lags in breathing.
Acid-fast mycobacteria in sputum (Ziehl–Neelsen stain), Xpert MTB/RIF (PCR), culture. Blood: lymphopenia, monocytosis, raised ESR. Diaskintest, IGRA (QuantiFERON).
X-ray and CT: infiltrate in the upper lobes, foci, a thick-walled cavity, a “draining bronchus”, calcifications. Fiberoptic bronchoscopy.
Pulmonary hemorrhage, spontaneous pneumothorax, tuberculous pleurisy and empyema, bronchial tuberculosis, amyloidosis, chronic cor pulmonale.
Difference from pneumonia: location in the upper lobes, slow course, no response to (non-TB) antibiotics, mycobacteria in the sputum.
Infiltrative tuberculosis (right apex)
The right supraclavicular fossa is sunken, the right side lags slightly in breathing.
Vocal fremitus slightly increased over the apex; Sternberg's sign — pain in the shoulder girdle muscles, Pottenger's sign — muscle rigidity on the affected side.
Impaired sound over the right apex; the height of the apex is reduced, Kronig's isthmus is narrowed.
Saccadic or mixed (bronchovesicular) breathing; fine consonating moist rales over the apex, audible after a short cough.
Tuberculous infiltrate
To detect fine moist rales the patient is told to exhale, cough briefly, and then breathe in deeply.
Cavitary tuberculosis (right upper lobe)
The upper part of the right half of the chest is sunken and lags in breathing.
Vocal fremitus is increased over the cavity.
Tympanic sound over the cavity (metallic or cracked-pot sound in a large cavity), with dullness around it.
Amphoric breathing, coarse and medium-bubble consonating moist rales.
Cavity
Pericavitary infiltration and fibrosis
Dry (fibrinous) pleurisy
Pleura
Deposition of fibrin on the pleural layers: stabbing pain related to breathing and a pleural friction rub; percussion is almost unchanged.
Inflammation of the pleural layers with deposition of fibrin on their surface; there is no significant fluid in the pleural cavity.
Pneumonia (parapneumonic), tuberculosis, viral infections, pulmonary infarction, connective tissue diseases (CTD), uremia, tumor, trauma.

The visceral and parietal layers, covered with rough fibrin, rub against each other in breathing movements: a pleural friction rub. The parietal pleura is rich in pain receptors, so the pain is related to breathing; the patient limits breathing because of the pain.

Stabbing pain in the side of the chest that worsens on inspiration, coughing, sneezing and bending toward the healthy side; dry cough, low-grade fever. In diaphragmatic pleurisy the pain is in the abdomen and radiates to the shoulder, with hiccups.
The patient lies on the painful side (movement is restricted), the affected side lags in breathing, and the breathing is shallow and rapid.
Moderate leukocytosis, raised ESR; tests according to the cause.
X-ray: the movement of the diaphragm dome is limited, and the costophrenic sinus may be blunted. Ultrasound: pleural thickening, a little fluid.
Progression to exudative pleurisy, pleural adhesions (adhesive bands).

Differentiate the pleural friction rub from crepitation and moist rales: it is heard in both phases, is not changed by coughing, intensifies when the stethoscope is pressed, and is heard even in “false breathing” with the abdomen while the mouth and nose are closed.
Clinical picture (right lower lateral area)
Lies on the painful side, the right side lags in breathing.

Pain on pressing the intercostal spaces; sometimes a rub is felt under the palm. Vocal fremitus unchanged. In diaphragmatic pleurisy, Mussy's sign: pain on pressing between the heads of the sternocleidomastoid muscle.
Clear lung sound; on the affected side the mobility of the lower edge is reduced.
Diminished vesicular breathing (because of the pain), a pleural friction rub, most often in the lower lateral area.
Pleura covered with fibrin
The rub intensifies when the stethoscope is pressed and does not change after coughing.
Exudative pleurisy and hydrothorax
Fluid in the pleural cavity: femoral dullness, no breath sounds or fremitus. The Damoiseau–Sokolov line, Garland's and Rauchfuss–Grocco triangles.

Accumulation of pathological fluid in the pleural cavity. An exudate is due to inflammation (protein >30 g/L, Light's criteria), a transudate (hydrothorax) to a disturbance of hydrostatic or oncotic pressure.
Exudate: parapneumonic, tuberculosis, tumor (metastases, mesothelioma), PE, CTD, pancreatitis. Transudate: heart failure (often bilateral or on the right), cirrhosis of the liver, nephrotic syndrome.

Fluid collects in the lower areas and compresses the lung upward and inward. In an exudate the upper border is oblique (the Damoiseau–Sokolov line: highest at the posterior axillary line), in a transudate more horizontal. A large amount of fluid displaces the mediastinum to the healthy side.
At the beginning pain in the side (the dry pleurisy stage); when fluid accumulates the pain decreases and heaviness in the chest and shortness of breath increase; dry cough, fever (in an exudate).

Forced position: lies on the affected side. The affected half of the chest is enlarged, the intercostal spaces are smoothed out or bulging, and it lags in breathing. Dyspnea, acrocyanosis; with a large amount of fluid the neck veins are full.
Pleural puncture: exudate (protein >30 g/L, pleural/serum protein >0.5, LDH >0.6; Rivalta test positive) or transudate; cell count, glucose, pH, culture, cytology, ADA (tuberculosis).

Ultrasound detects fluid from 50 mL and marks the puncture site. X-ray: blunting of the costophrenic sinus in the upright position (from 200–300 mL), a homogeneous opacity with an oblique upper border, mediastinal shift. CT: to find the cause.
Pleural empyema, adhesions and fibrothorax, respiratory failure.

Difference from obstructive atelectasis: the chest half is enlarged and the mediastinum is displaced to the healthy side (in atelectasis it is reduced and displaced to the affected side). Difference from lobar pneumonia: fremitus and bronchophony are weakened.
Exudative pleurisy (left, moderate volume)
The left half of the chest is enlarged, the intercostal spaces are smoothed out, it lags in breathing; the apex beat is displaced to the right.
Resistance increased; vocal fremitus is not detected over the fluid and is increased over the compressed lung above it.

Dull (femoral) sound over the fluid with an oblique upper border: the Damoiseau–Sokolov line. Dull-tympanic sound in Garland's triangle; dullness in the Rauchfuss–Grocco triangle on the healthy side. Skodaic tympany above the fluid level. On the left, Traube's space disappears. Mobility of the lower edge is not detected.

Breathing over the fluid is sharply diminished or inaudible; faint bronchial breathing and egophony at the fluid border and in Garland's triangle; sometimes a pleural friction rub (at the fluid border).
Not detected over the fluid, increased over the compressed lung.
Fluid on the left abolishes Traube's space (dullness).
Hydrothorax (bilateral, heart failure)
Orthopnea, leg edema, full neck veins; the lower part of the chest is widened on both sides.
Vocal fremitus in the lower areas is weakened on both sides or not detected.
Bilateral dull sound in the lower areas, the upper border almost horizontal (transudate), usually higher on the right; mobility not detected.
Breathing in the lower areas is sharply diminished or inaudible; higher up, fine non-consonating moist rales because of congestion.
Diminished in the lower areas.
Pneumothorax
Air in the pleural cavity: unilateral tympanic sound, no breath sounds or fremitus. A valvular (tension) pneumothorax is an emergency.
Air enters the pleural cavity and the lung partly or completely collapses.

Primary spontaneous: tall, thin young men, rupture of subpleural apical bullae, smoking. Secondary: COPD, asthma, tuberculosis, pneumocystosis, cystic fibrosis. Traumatic and iatrogenic (puncture, central venous catheter, mechanical ventilation).

The negative pleural pressure is lost and the lung collapses toward the hilum through its elastic recoil. Closed — the airflow has stopped; open — the cavity communicates with the outside or with a bronchus; valvular (tension) — with each inspiration air enters and does not leave: the pressure rises, the mediastinum is pushed to the healthy side, and venous return decreases.
Suddenly, often on exertion, sharp stabbing pain on the affected side (radiating to the shoulder), shortness of breath, dry cough, a feeling of fear.

The affected half of the chest is enlarged, does not take part in breathing, and the intercostal spaces are smoothed out. Tachypnea, cyanosis. In a tension pneumothorax: full neck veins, hypotension, tachycardia, the trachea displaced to the healthy side; subcutaneous emphysema (crepitus on palpation).
Arterial blood gases: hypoxemia.
X-ray (upright, in normal breathing): the line of the visceral pleura, with no lung markings beyond it. Ultrasound: loss of “lung sliding”, the “lung point”. CT: bullae.
Tension pneumothorax, hemopneumothorax, pyopneumothorax, recurrence, re-expansion edema.
Difference from emphysema: unilateral signs and sudden onset; CT to distinguish from a large bulla.
Closed pneumothorax (right)
The right half of the chest is enlarged and does not take part in breathing.
Vocal fremitus is not detected; no excursion.
Tympanic sound (hyperresonant or metallic if the air pressure is high); the lower border of the right lung is not detected; liver dullness is displaced downward.
Breath sounds are sharply diminished or inaudible.
Diminished or not detected.
Open pneumothorax (communicating with a bronchus)
The same as in a closed one; in an open wound, a “sucking” sound of air.
Fremitus is not detected.
Tympanic sound.
Amphoric breathing (air enters and leaves through the bronchial opening); sometimes a “falling drop” sound (in hydropneumothorax).
Valvular (tension) pneumothorax
Severe dyspnea, cyanosis, full neck veins, hypotension, the trachea displaced to the left. Urgent decompression is required!
No fremitus; in subcutaneous emphysema, crepitus (a snow-like crunch).
High tympanic or metallic sound; cardiac dullness displaced to the left.
No breath sounds are heard.
Not detected.
Obstructive atelectasis
The bronchus is blocked and the lobe loses its air and shrinks: dull sound, no breath sounds or fremitus, the chest half is reduced and the mediastinum is pulled toward the affected side.
Collapse of the alveoli because air in the part of the lung supplied by the bronchus is absorbed after the bronchial lumen is blocked.
Central lung cancer (the most common), foreign body (in children), mucus or blood plug (after surgery, in severely ill patients), bronchial carcinoid, compression by enlarged lymph nodes.

Air distal to the blocked bronchus is absorbed into the blood, the lobe loses its air and shrinks in volume. Negative pressure pulls the mediastinum, diaphragm and ribs toward the affected side. Because the bronchus is closed, sound and vibration do not reach the chest wall.
Shortness of breath (when the atelectasis is large and develops quickly), dry cough; with a tumor: hemoptysis, weight loss, prolonged cough.
The affected half of the chest is reduced, the intercostal spaces are drawn in, and it lags in breathing.
According to the cause: tumor markers, sputum cytology.
X-ray: homogeneous opacity with reduced lobar volume, displaced fissures, mediastinum shifted toward the affected side, raised diaphragm. Bronchoscopy is the key test (cause and treatment). CT.
Obstructive pneumonia, abscess, bronchiectasis.

Difference from exudative pleurisy: the chest half is reduced and the mediastinum is displaced toward the affected side (in pleurisy, toward the healthy side). Difference from lobar pneumonia: no fremitus or bronchophony, no breath sounds.
Atelectasis of the right lower lobe
The lower part of the right half of the chest is sunken and lags in breathing; the trachea and heart are displaced to the right.
Vocal fremitus is not detected over the atelectasis.
Dull sound; the right lower border is raised, and mobility is reduced.
No breath sounds (in incomplete obstruction: diminished breathing, sometimes a localized wheeze).
Airless lobe
Pulmonary congestion and edema
Circulation
In left ventricular failure: bilateral non-consonating fine moist rales in the lower areas; in alveolar edema: coarse “bubbling” over the whole lung.

Because of left ventricular or left atrial failure, the pressure in the pulmonary capillaries rises and fluid passes into the interstitium (interstitial congestion) and then into the alveoli (alveolar edema).
Myocardial infarction, arterial hypertension, cardiomyopathies, aortic valve disease, mitral stenosis, arrhythmias, hypertensive crisis.

Interstitial edema when the pressure exceeds 18–25 mm Hg, alveolar edema above 25. Fluid collects first in the lower posterior areas by gravity. Edema of the bronchial mucosa causes bronchospasm (“cardiac asthma”).

Shortness of breath on exertion, then at rest, orthopnea (sleeps on several pillows), nocturnal attacks of suffocation (cardiac asthma), dry cough; in acute edema: suffocation, pink frothy sputum, fear of death.
Orthopneic position, acrocyanosis, cold sweat. In acute edema, “boiling samovar” breathing audible from a distance, pink foam from the mouth.
NT-proBNP or BNP raised; troponin (in infarction); blood gases: hypoxemia.
X-ray: venous congestion, Kerley B lines, peribronchial cuffing, “butterfly” perihilar opacity, pleural fluid. ECG, echocardiography (ejection fraction, valves), lung ultrasound (B lines).
Cardiogenic shock, respiratory failure, hydrothorax.

Difference from pneumonia: the signs are bilateral and symmetric, there is no fever, and there are signs of heart disease; difference from bronchial asthma: the cardiac history and moist rales in the lower areas.
Interstitial congestion (chronic heart failure)
Orthopnea, acrocyanosis, leg edema.
Bilateral impaired sound in the lower posterior areas, mobility reduced.
Bilateral symmetric non-consonating fine-bubble moist rales and crepitation in the lower areas; not reduced after coughing. In “cardiac asthma”, dry rales.
Congestion
Non-consonating fine moist rales: the lung tissue is not consolidated, so the sound is conducted weakly.
Alveolar pulmonary edema (acute)
Forced sitting position, severe suffocation, cyanosis, cold sweat, pink frothy sputum, noisy breathing audible from a distance.
Tachycardia; fremitus unchanged.
Dullness in the lower areas; a hyperresonant tinge above is possible.
First over the lower areas, then over the whole lung: moist rales of different caliber (fine, medium, coarse); “bubbling” audible from a distance.
Alveolar edema
The alveoli and bronchi are filled with frothy fluid: moist rales of different caliber.
Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis
Progressive fibrosis of the interstitium: end-inspiratory “Velcro” fine rales in the lower posterior areas, a shrunken lung.
A chronic progressive fibrosing interstitial pneumonia of unknown cause, seen mainly in older patients, with the morphology of usual interstitial pneumonia (UIP).
Cause unknown; risk factors: smoking, old age, male sex, metal and wood dust, gastroesophageal reflux, genetic predisposition (MUC5B, telomerase genes).

Repeated injury of the alveolar epithelium and fibroblast foci: collagen accumulates, the lung becomes stiff and shrinks (restriction), with “honeycomb” changes. The sudden opening of stiff alveoli at the end of inspiration gives dry, fine rales resembling sticky tape.
Gradually increasing shortness of breath on exertion, dry tormenting cough, weakness, weight loss.
Clubbed fingers (up to 50%), cyanosis, tachypnea, shallow breathing; the chest is reduced in size.
Autoimmune markers (to exclude CTD); blood gases: desaturation on exertion.

High-resolution CT is the key test: subpleural, basal reticular changes, “honeycombing”, traction bronchiectasis. Spirometry: restriction (FVC reduced, FEV1/FVC normal or increased), DLCO reduced. 6-minute walk test.
Respiratory failure, pulmonary hypertension, chronic cor pulmonale, lung cancer, acute exacerbation.
Difference from congestion in heart failure: the rales are dry, end-inspiratory, with a “Velcro” timbre, and are not changed by diuretics; clubbed fingers, restriction.
Clubbed fingers, tachypnea, reduced chest excursion.
Excursion reduced; vocal fremitus unchanged or slightly increased.
Impaired sound in the lower areas; the lower borders are raised, and mobility is reduced.
Bilateral end-inspiratory “Velcro”-type fine rales (crepitation) in the lower posterior and lateral areas, not changed by coughing; vesicular breathing diminished.
Unchanged or slightly increased.
Fibrosis (UIP)
“Velcro” rales belong to the group of fine moist rales (recording: fine moist rales).
Pulmonary embolism and pulmonary infarction
Sudden shortness of breath and tachycardia; physical signs are often scanty. If an infarction develops: localized dullness, moist rales and a pleural friction rub.

Blockage of the pulmonary artery or its branches by a thrombus (most often from the deep veins of the legs). Pulmonary infarction is hemorrhagic necrosis of lung tissue when a peripheral branch is blocked.
Virchow's triad: venous stasis (immobilization, surgery, long travel), hypercoagulability (tumor, pregnancy, estrogens, thrombophilia), vessel wall injury (trauma).
Dead space that is ventilated but not perfused: hypoxemia, tachypnea; acute right ventricular strain. In infarction the alveoli fill with blood (consolidation), and the pleura is involved.
Sudden shortness of breath, pleuritic chest pain, cough, hemoptysis (in infarction), palpitations, fainting; leg swelling and pain (deep vein thrombosis).
Tachypnea, tachycardia, cyanosis (in massive PE: of the face and upper body), full neck veins, hypotension; swelling of one leg.
D-dimer raised (excludes it at low probability), troponin and NT-proBNP (right ventricular injury), blood gases: hypoxemia, hypocapnia.

CT pulmonary angiography is key. ECG: sinus tachycardia, SI–QIII–TIII, right bundle branch block. Echocardiography: right ventricular dilatation. Ultrasound of the leg veins. Probability scores: Wells, Geneva.
Obstructive shock, sudden death, infarct pneumonia, pleurisy, chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension.
Difference from pneumonia: sudden onset, risk factors, dyspnea out of proportion to the physical signs; difference from myocardial infarction: ECG, troponin dynamics, CT angiography.
PE (without infarction)
Tachypnea, cyanosis, full neck veins.
Tachycardia; vocal fremitus unchanged.
Usually unchanged.
Often unchanged or locally diminished breathing; over the heart, accentuated and split S2 over the pulmonary artery.
Pulmonary infarction (right lower lobe)
Pleuritic pain, hemoptysis, the affected side lags in breathing.
Vocal fremitus is increased over the infarct.
Impaired or dull sound over the infarct.
Diminished or bronchial breathing, fine moist rales, a pleural friction rub.
Hemorrhagic infarct (wedge-shaped)
A pleural friction rub is also heard (separate button below).
Upper airway obstruction
Narrowing of the larynx or trachea: inspiratory dyspnea and stridor audible from a distance — an emergency.
Difficulty of air passage caused by narrowing of the lumen of the larynx or trachea; acute (minutes to hours) or chronic.

Foreign body, laryngeal edema (anaphylaxis, Quincke's edema), croup and epiglottitis (in children), tumor of the larynx or trachea, post-intubation stenosis, vocal cord paralysis, compression by a goiter.

Fast airflow through the narrowed part sets the walls vibrating and produces a high-pitched monophonic sound — stridor. An extrathoracic narrowing collapses on inspiration (inspiratory stridor), an intrathoracic tracheal narrowing on expiration.
Difficulty breathing, noisy breathing, hoarseness or aphonia, cough (with a foreign body: sudden, during eating), suffocation.
Inspiratory dyspnea: inspiration is prolonged, and the jugular, supraclavicular and intercostal fossae are drawn in on inspiration; forced position with the head thrown back, cyanosis, restlessness.
Blood gases: hypoxemia, hypercapnia (late).
Laryngoscopy and bronchoscopy (cause and foreign body removal), CT of the neck and chest, flow–volume loop (flattened).
Asphyxia, hypoxic brain injury, cardiac arrest.
Difference from bronchial asthma: stridor is on inspiration, loudest over the neck, monophonic; in asthma the wheeze is polyphonic, in expiration, over the chest.
Laryngeal stenosis
Inspiratory dyspnea, drawing in of the fossae on inspiration, cyanosis.
The larynx descends on inspiration; fremitus unchanged.
High-pitched monophonic stridor, loudest over the trachea, conducted over the whole chest; vesicular breathing diminished.
